items.title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
items.content: At a glance Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for.  PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line.  The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it. Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation.  This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an…

items.title: [AINews] LLMs can read & write neural network weights: "Weight Space Programming" cuts Autoresearch out of the RSI loop
items.content: Amid a deepening bear market for AI/tech (worthy of dark humor ) with Anthropic bonds receiving a “junk” rating and OpenAI fundraise headlines , we continue to see very surprising capability finds in the community, such as today. The best way to put today’s blockbuster paper in context is to recall Karpathy’s autoresearch from a mere 8 months ago , which presaged a summer of recursive self improvement fears : Abstractly, the demonstration is that you can take a sufficiently smart model and through running a series of experiments across a compute cluster, train a model autonomously without human expertise or intervention. However, this is usually done by an involved process of writing PyTorch/Jax code and running compute and watching loss curves and reading evals and optimizing kernels and data and…. Well, last month’s guest Alex Zhang comes back to coauthor a MONSTER discovery: what if you just ask a smart model to directly read and edit the weights of a dumber model? View post on X ↗ In ML this is the equivalent of not looking at source code, just directly seeing the 1’s and 0’s of ( very small ) compiled executables, and being able to 1) tell what they do , 2) oneshot-fix bugs given failed traces or, with 50 steps, improve in a general direction ( possible overstatement here ), 3) writing entire network weights from scratch in one shot , beating some independently trained models. If you believe that LLMs can truly fit and simulate everything given enough parameters (and in fact, LLMs are increasingly better calculators as you grow in size), then something like this was in theory bound to happen, but it is surprising nevertheless to have the ability suddenly emerge, as an independent reproduction seems to already have found: View post on X ↗ Of course the exact thing we are really modeling is some variant of mechanistic interpretability (which could be done by hand ), and right now unlikely to scale to more advanced tasks than simple games and RL policies, but the…

items.title: Building Legal Agents When You Can't See the Data - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
items.content: Legora can’t read a single trace of what its agent does for a lawyer. The data belongs to the law firm’s clients. How do you build and test an agent when you can’t see its work? Jacob Lauritzen is the CTO of Legora, one of the fastest-growing companies in legal tech history. The team started in a Stockholm basement with ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Today, a lawyer can use Legora to draft and edit Word documents, review 10,000 contracts in a single table, or run due diligence. The agent also coordinates work between lawyers, clients, and other agents. When Legora made its own acquisitions, the team used it for diligence. What we talked about • Why Legora resisted adding a model picker for years, and why it finally added one • Jacob’s estimate that models already do about 60% of legal work well, and why the rest takes a smarter model • How three engineers and three lawyers build test environments modeled on customers’ work, much like the “worlds” used in reinforcement learning • A citation problem where the model got it right 70% of the time, then 99% after one release. Legora didn’t have to change anything. • Why Legora runs everything on Azure and why it doesn’t use ElevenLabs • Tabular Review, the million-cell spreadsheet the industry copied down to the name • How intake works, how agents create lists, and how a list can start another agent • What legal engineers and forward-deployed engineers each do, and who gets to write code • The 300 Spartans slide Jacob used to argue that 20 engineers would be enough forever. Now there are 100, and he still feels short-handed. • Why Jacob finds Fable and Opus too chatty for drafting and likes Astra’s concise writing • Why drafting a long contract is a search problem • Whether model labs will cut off legal tools the way they cut off coding tools • What happens to law firm partnerships, the billable hour, and jobs for junior lawyers Legora is hiring engineers in New York, Stockholm, and London. items.title: Xi vs Trump on Corruption
items.content: In February, Eric and Donald Jr. sat down with a reporter to explain why Abu Dhabi paid $500m for a stake in World Liberty Financial. Don Jr. said, “They tried all this nonsense the first time around. Frankly, it’s gotten old…They created this monster.” The monster of political corruption has been with us since the founding. But since the Progressive Eva, it has been cut with at least a tinge of embarrassment. The Trumps instead have done it in broad daylight and tried to make it a flex. China’s political system is riddled with corruption on an entirely different scale. The skims in China happen up and down the system, and making a billion dollars while in office is nothing new for senior Chinese leaders. But Xi understands what this costs the Party. In his first Politburo speech as General Secretary, he warned that corruption, left to spread, would “doom the Party and the state.” Xi was horrified by seeing youth with bloodlines just as red as his crash foreign sports cars in the streets of Beijing. He views the princeling inheritance as a responsibility to serve, not a license to fuckboy. As Kamil Galeev writes , Xi aims to extirpate “the alien, unfamiliar, threatening bandit entrepreneurial culture — not even from the country but rather, from the national elites.” Xi is a believer, but Trump is a businessman. After Trump brought down the guardrails with a compliant SCOTUS and Congress, the presidential family has been sloppily revenue-maximizing ever since. 1 Xi’s anti-corruption campaign hasn’t liquidated corruption in China, which still lubricates a much higher percentage of economic activity than similar behavior does in America. But Xi has succeeded in making it dangerous. Making outside money in Xi’s China runs the risk of execution — far different stakes than embarrassing ProPublica articles revealing crimes that get pardoned away. Make corruption cringe again! items.title: Ep 95: Modal CEO on the Future of Inference, the Chaos of the GPU Market & Origins of the Sandbox Bet
items.content: Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:04 How much of, like, an an organized marketplaces compute these days versus, like, the Wild West? Speaker 2 | 00:04 - 00:17 I went to GTC last year. It was like an open air drug market, but, like, GPUs. Walking around, like, talking to people, trying to get GPUs, and meeting people in hotel lobbies, exchanging numbers. It's very far from an efficient market. I mean, some people are working on this. Speaker 2 | 00:17 - 00:29 Compute comes in many different shapes or forms. I also feel like structurally, it will be a little bit, like, sort of unwieldy for a long time. Like, it's just not something you can, like, sort of buy and sell in an exchange because it's not like a fungible contract. Speaker 3 | 00:34 - 00:48 Welcome to unsupervised learning. As you can probably tell from my voice, I am not Jacob. I am Patrick Chase, GP at Redpoint. So awesome to have Eric on unsupervised learning for the second time. He is the founder and CEO at Modal. Speaker 3 | 00:48 - 01:14 I have learned so much from working with him over the last three years. He is one of my favorite people to jam on AI ideas with. He has an incredible ability to move seamlessly from the lowest altitude of developer shipping code to the highest altitude of where the market is going and building what is missing. We talk about the mobile journey over the last three years, the crazy technology they have built to make it all work, inference, sandboxes, and what's coming next. Hope you enjoy the episode. Speaker 3 | 01:15 - 01:28 For you guys, there is obviously a ton of AI compute demand and lots of people going out and trying to reserve, you know, GPUs and CPUs. What's it like for you guys finding compute in in the market today? Speaker 2 | 01:29 - 01:49 It's pretty rough. Mean, like, you know, not rough in the sense that like we can actually find compute. I think there's a little bit of a misconception that like we're sort of... We are certainly scarce, you know, in terms of compute in certain ways, but like there is capacity you can get. You just have to look a little bit further, accept higher prices, accept longer terms, etcetera. Speaker 2 | 01:49 - 02:10 And and we do that a lot. I mean, probably do like two compute deals every week at this point, if not three. And and so we we keep to, you know, stacking up, you know, more and more compute. And and I really think that's the beauty of model is we can aggregate all this demand and and manage the capacity in aggregate much more efficiently. And and the value prop of model has always been like, don't think of my capacity. Speaker 2 | 02:10 - 02:18 Like, we had a lot of that, like, annoying stuff to sort of the day to day knife fighting of of getting capacity and working... items.title: [AINews] Building AIE CODE: The top Coding Agent Conference
items.content: It’s a quiet day, so as we have done once per conference, we’ll do a behind the scenes look at AI Engineer , now serving 6M views a month for 1.8M monthly unique viewers . CODE is the last flagship AIE of the year (there are also 2 partner conferences coming up - AIEi Shanghai takes place next week, and AIEi Sydney is a side event of NeurIPS in December). As a Summit it is meant to be more intimate: single track, invite-only for the top 1000 agentic engineers in the world (over 100k tuned into our Software Factories track at WF26 ). My goal in curating AIE CODE is to try to recap the top themes of 2026 in code and gather the leaders of the industry to preview what’s next in 2027. Last year we had some absolute bangers building Skills and Software Factories , predicting the death of the IDE and of course the launch of Antigravity and Nano Banana Pro. We have three themes this year: Scaling without Slop : Last year’s call for No More Slop has resulted in lots of discussions about managing it this year, including the rise and fall of Tokenmaxxing . Our Scaling without Slop approach has mostly worked; we need more. System One models : We believe S1 “smart software” is the largest change to AI Engineering that refreshingly explores the opposite direction to ever larger and more expensive and questionably productive swarms of coding agent FactoryFactoryFactories. While Diogo took pains to explain the difference between Decision Models and System One models on our podcast and his WF26 talk , it has largely been lost to the broader audience. Diogo and team TypeSafe are back for a mini “Jev Day” to show how System One models are truly being used by their top users. Increasing Ambition: This year we also saw increasingly ambitious rewrites of some of the hardest categories of software, from browsers to Adobe PhotoShop Suite to mid-tier B2B SaaS . items.title: Why Agents Love Supabase
items.content: I first met Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson in Singapore, shortly after they finished YC as the hottest startup of YC S20 . Six years later, we finally got them on the podcast! This is their first podcast together, after taking an open-source, fully remote company from zero to a $10 billion valuation. The title is a question I wanted to understand for myself: why do agents love Supabase? There are plenty of managed databases. Postgres hosting is competitive. Being familiar to a model is useful distribution, but it doesn't explain all the work needed to turn a generated application into something that runs. But when I ran my frontier AEO tracker , it was an almost complete sweep of first choice for app backends (and in contention for managed db ) for every frontier model from Astra to Fable to Muse. At Select, Supabase grouped its announcements into Build, Operate and Scale. The things that stood out to me were surprisingly practical: start a local backend without Docker, keep the desired database schema in Git, and run compute beside the database. Each removes a piece of work that developers have been doing for years. Agents make that friction harder to ignore. Watch the full conversation, including my opening commentary → Give the agent a backend it can read My favorite developer-tool announcements make me think: of course I want this today. The new alpha runtime for running Supabase locally without Docker is one of those. I use Colima rather than Docker Desktop, and even then, removing another dependency from the path to a working database is welcome. Local setup is a small part of a human developer's week; an agent that repeatedly creates and tests environments encounters it over and over. Declarative schemas are the bigger idea. The familiar SQL workflow accumulates a history: create the schema, then migrate, migrate, migrate. A declarative representation gives the agent a description of the state you want, in files it can inspect and edit alongside the applica…
